about: The words of CHAIN rollo_911 (Data/encounters/chain_rollo_911_793.json; Design/content/chains/rollo_911.md): the Seine in the hands of the Northmen and Rollo made lord at Rotomagus, 904 to 918. Every title, intention, line and label the cards use; an outcome text for every option (out_<option>, and out_<option>_fail where there is a chance); three news items; an art line for each of the fourteen cards. Nothing is quoted: Dudo and Flodoard are retold in our own words. Invented people: Ketil, Gozbert, Odilard, Warin, Thorstein. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Nobody goes to Rouen
A skipper in from the Channel is selling his news for the price of listening. It is about the Seine, which honest ships have left to the Northmen for a lifetime.
Nobody goes up to Rouen. Everybody says so, and so everybody stays away, and so the three boats that do go are paid like bishops.
The heathen men have sat on that river since before my beard came. They do not burn the town now. They live in it. A man called Rollo keeps them, more or less.
An army eats. They have the silver of every church between the sea and Burgundy, and nothing to spend it on but bread and wine.
Blades and horses are another matter. The old king's law is death for that, and it is the one law on that river that still works.
Ask what bread fetches under the wall
Buy him ale and ask how a keel gets up there
Leave Rouen to those three boats
Half as much again as anywhere on the Channel, he says, and paid in good silver with church dust still on it. Wheat, rye, anything that will bake.

Two cups later you have it. Wait in the river mouth for the flood, ride it up, and tie to the bank when it leaves you; the tide reaches the town wall. And wine is cheap at Rouen, because nobody dares fetch it away.
He shrugs and tells it to the next man. The river will still be there.

A Channel strand on a grey afternoon: a weathered skipper on an upturned tub, a cup in his hand, pointing south-west with his thumb over a row of beached boats; two listeners, one already turning away.
The ruined market

Rotomagus stands, in the way a burned house stands. The Roman wall is whole on the river side; behind it the market place is grass. Long ships lie under the wall where the wine boats lay. Two men come down to your boat from two directions.
Ketil. I buy for the camp. You are the first cargo this moon that came of its own will.
I pay in silver by weight, a little over what a Frank would give, because a Frank would not come. Do not ask where the silver was before.
Gozbert, of the archbishop's house. We are still here. People forget that. The archbishop, eleven canons, and the poor, who had nowhere to run to.
Sell to him and you feed the wolf. Sell to us and you feed what the wolf left. We pay less. I will not pretend otherwise.
I am the wine trade of Rouen. All of it. My father had forty casks a week through that gate. I have a cellar and a door that locks.
Sell to the Northmen's steward
Carry your wares up to the archbishop's house
Sell nothing yet. Walk the town with the wine seller

Ketil weighs out hacked silver and half the foot of a chalice against your goods, and adds thirty pennies' weight for the coming. His men carry everything up through the river gate. Nobody on the strand looks at you, which is its own kind of look.
The canon pays twelve pennies over nothing much and has your name written down. The bread goes out at the church door the same evening. Ketil watches you pass and says nothing at all.

Odilard shows you the town in an hour: the two churches with a gallery between them, the empty places where the saints lay before they were carried inland, the old theatre where the Northmen keep horses. Wine here goes at three parts in four of the Paris price, he says, for want of keels to take it to sea.

Rotomagus from the water at low morning light: a long Roman wall of patched grey stone, six long ships drawn up under it, grass and a few goats where a market was; a fair-haired steward with an arm ring and a thin canon in black walking down to one small boat from opposite sides.
The canon's errand
Gozbert finds you on the strand before Prime with a folded sheet sealed in wax. The archbishop wants a letter taken up the river to Count Robert at Paris.
It asks the count for grain for the city's poor before the winter. That is the part I may tell you.

The other part says what the Northmen might take, if a king were to offer it, in place of what they take now. My lord has baptised a few of them. He thinks more would stand still for it if they had ground to stand on.
A clerk on the road is searched by everybody. A boat with casks is only taxed.
The priest has a letter. I would give forty pennies to know what a priest writes to a count about us. I would not need to keep it.
Carry the letter to Paris unopened
Carry it, and let Ketil hear it read first
You carry casks, not letters
You put it in the dry place under the stern board, with the weights. He gives ten pennies for the way and his blessing, in that order.
Ketil has a captive deacon read it to him twice, nods, and has the seal mended with a hot knife so that it nearly fits. Forty pennies. 'He writes well of us,' he says. 'Better than we would.'
He nods like a man who has been refused by better. A boy goes with the letter by the road next morning, on a mule. You hear later that the mule arrived.

Before sunrise on the river strand, mist on the water: the canon holding out a small folded letter with a red wax seal to the merchant in his boat; far behind, on the wall, one Northman on watch looking down at them.
The count's man
On the strand at Parisius a man in a good mail shirt asks every boat where she has come from. When you say Rotomagus he sends his groom away and sits down on your gunwale.
Warin. I serve Count Robert, who holds this river for the king as far down as he can hold it. That is not as far as Rouen.
The letter I will take. The archbishop shall have his grain. My lord does not let a city starve because he cannot reach it.
This seal has been warmed. I will not ask by whom. I will ask you something else instead.
How many keels under the wall? How many men who can stand? Horses? You have eyes and a tally stick. I pay for both.
My lord's brother held this city against them for eleven months when I was a boy. I carried water on the wall. Nobody needs to tell me what they are.
Tell him what you counted
A merchant counts casks, not ships
Double the ships and let him pay for the fright

You give him the count: the ships, the horse lines in the old theatre, the cook fires at dusk. He marks it on a wax board and pays a hundred pennies of Paris, new and sharp. 'Come again,' he says. 'Count again.'

He looks at you a while. 'Then count casks,' he says, and tells you where: the vine growers above the city sell low this year, with nobody to carry their wine to sea. He leaves twenty pennies on the thwart, for the road or for nothing, and goes.
He writes down twice what you saw and pays for it gladly: a hundred and forty pennies. A frightened count buys no battle this year. You wonder, going down the strand, which side you have just helped.
He lets you finish. 'A boatman from Jumièges counted for me at Whitsun,' he says. 'He counted half that.' Twenty pennies, for the road. He does not sit on your gunwale again.

The Paris strand at noon, the island and its wall behind: a broad man in mail and a red cloak sitting sideways on the gunwale of a small boat, a wax tablet on his knee, the merchant standing among his casks counting on his fingers.
Blades and horses
Ketil does not come down to the boat this time. He sends for you, to the bishop's old storehouse, where the camp's silver lies in a heap like turnips.
Bread I have. I want Frankish blades, the kind with a name in the iron, and horses that will carry a man in mail. I pay three times the market.
I know your law. Death for the seller. The old king said it at Pîtres, the same summer he built his bridge. The bridge did not stop us either.
You have iron under those hides now. I can smell the grease.
My cousin sold them four horses in the year of the long siege. The count's men hanged him at the bridge, over the water, where the boats could see. Ketil will not tell you that part.
Promise him the iron and horses you carry
Offer wheat instead, as much as he wants
Nothing the king hangs for

He weighs out two hundred and fifty pennies above whatever the market gives you, now, before the goods have left your hold. There is no writing of it. There is Odilard, who saw, and Odilard has a cousin's widow at Paris.

He is not pleased and not surprised. Six loads of wheat within the half year, at well over the market: he cuts a tally for it and splits it with you. 'A careful man,' he says. It is not praise, and not blame.
'Then you will live long,' Ketil says, 'and thinly.' But he tells you one thing for nothing: the camp is short of salt for the autumn killing, and will pay for it.

Inside a stone storehouse lit by one door: a heap of hacked silver, cups and book mounts on the floor; the steward crouched beside it with a folding balance, holding up one Frankish sword blade to the light; the merchant in the doorway, the wine seller's face at his shoulder.
After Chartres

This year the Northmen of the Seine sat down before Chartres. On the Saturday before the Magdalen's Mass Count Robert and Duke Richard came upon them, and the bishop showed the Lady's shift from the wall, and very many heathen men were killed. What is left has come home to Rotomagus.
We were beaten. There: a thing few of us will say twice. Fewer ships came back than went, and the men in them eat as much as ever.
The country will sell us nothing now it has seen us run. I need bread on trust until the leaves fall. Rollo does not forget who fed him. Nor who did not.
My lord says it is now or not in our lifetime. A beaten man will hear terms. He is sending me up the river to the king's people, and I need a boat that is only taxed.
I know who heard my lord's last letter read. I am asking you all the same. There is nobody else with a boat.
Or a man might go up to Paris and tell the count how few they are, and how hungry. One hard autumn and the river would be clean. I only say what a man might do.
Buy the camp its bread on your own purse
Take the archbishop's clerk up the river
Go up to Paris with what you know

Sixty pennies of rye and barley, bought dear from farms that would not sell to them. Ketil counts every loaf and says a short word in his own tongue to the men who carry it. They look at you differently after.

Gozbert sits in the bows with his hood up through two days of rain and one of sun. At the king's landing he is met by men who were expecting him. He is gone four days and comes back thinner and nearly cheerful.
You say nothing on the strand and cast off on the morning flood. Odilard watches you go. Behind you the cook fires are fewer than at midsummer. You count them, from habit.

The strand under the wall of Rotomagus on a dull late-summer evening: fewer ships than before, two of them scorched; bandaged men sitting against the stones round three small cook fires; the steward, the canon and the wine seller all standing at one small boat.
The ford on the Epte

At the leaf fall the king and the Northmen meet where a road fords the Epte, the king's people on one bank and Rollo's on the other. Your boat is one of those that carry them up to the river's mouth. You wait three days with the keels and hear the rest from those who come back.
It is done. The city and the land about it down to the sea, to hold of the king. Baptism. And he keeps the river against every other fleet. My lord wept. I counted the witnesses.
They wanted him to kiss the king's foot. He would not bend. So one of ours did it for him, standing, and brought the foot up to his mouth. The king went over on his back. Some of them laughed.
That is how it is told already. I was holding horses. Tell it as you like.
Rollo looks at your boat, then at you. He says six words to Ketil, and Ketil makes them Frankish: 'The river is his now. Boats that fed it are his guests.'
He says one thing more, and Ketil does not need to turn it: your name, nearly right.
Ask what a keel pays on his river now
Ask the clerk to write your name in the archbishop's roll
Ask nothing. Mend sail and listen

Ketil asks. The answer is short: what she paid the king, and half of that for half a year for the boats that came when nobody came. He has it cut on a stick, since the clerks have gone home. Thirty pennies for the carrying.

Gozbert writes it on the way down, on his knee, in a hand the river shakes. He reads it to you mark by mark. It is the first time you have seen your own name and known which stroke was which. Thirty pennies for the carrying.
You hear the story of the foot four times before Rotomagus and it is better each time. The men are in good heart, yours among them. Thirty pennies for the carrying.

A small river joining a great one under yellow autumn trees: boats tied in a row at the bank, the merchant mending sail in his; coming down the path, a very big grey-bearded Northman in a Frankish cloak, his steward half a step behind, and a canon clutching a roll.
The bridge at Pîtres
Warin takes you up from the strand to a hall on the island, where a big tired man is eating with his mail still on. Count Robert asks his questions himself.
The king's counsellors say: give the Northman Rouen, which we do not hold, and let him guard it. My lord says: why pay a beaten man? It hangs on how beaten.
The old king's bridge at Pîtres still has its piers. Timber it, man it, and nothing that floats goes down to them or comes up from the sea. An army that cannot eat goes elsewhere. They always have.
You gave me a number once that a boatman from Jumièges halved. So today we will have it slowly, and twice.
There is talk of a keel that sold iron under the wall. I have not asked which. Speak well today and I shall not have to.
So. Ships that will swim. Men who can stand. Days of bread. Take your time. I have fought them since I was sixteen and I can wait another cup.
Tell him all of it: the ships, the bread, the sick
Tell him, and ask that those who go down river are let go
Say they are stronger than he hopes

You tell it. The count stops eating. Before you are back on the strand carpenters have been called for, and a rider has gone to the king to say: grant nothing, wait for the frost. A hundred and fifty pennies. The purse is heavier than it should be.

He hears the first part and frowns at the second. 'Down the river and out to sea, with their women, and nothing burned behind them. Yes. I want them gone, not dead. Dead costs men.' He has it said before witnesses. Eighty pennies.

You hear yourself say it: the walls sound, the ships many, the bread enough. He looks at you, then at Warin, and shrugs like a man who expected little. The king's counsellors will have their way. You go back down the river to see what comes of it.

A timber hall by lamplight: a heavy grey-haired count in mail at a table with bread, a knife and a cup, leaning forward on his elbows; his man standing behind with a wax board; the merchant facing them, cap in hand, the river dark in the open door.
Seven days in white

This year Rollo was baptised at Rotomagus by the archbishop, and Count Robert stood for him at the water and gave him his own name. For seven days he wears the white, and each day he gives land to a church. The town is full, for the first time since your grandfather's day.
Rollo passes in white linen, with a cross on a cord that he keeps touching, as a man touches a new tooth. He is very big and no longer young.

Our Lady's here, Our Lady's at Bayeux, Our Lady's at Evreux, Saint Michael's in the sea, Saint Peter's by our wall, Saint Peter's at Jumièges, Saint Denis's. Seven days, seven gifts. Much of it land he took from them himself. I do not say so this week.

On the eighth day he takes off the white and we get ours. The land is measured with a rope, and every man who followed him has a length of it. I am to have a farm. I do not know what one does with a farm.
Half the camp went into the water behind him. Some went in twice, for the shirt. Good linen is not given away every day.
Forty casks. I have sold forty casks since Sunday, and I have had to hire back my own father's cooper.
Buy white linen for the men who follow him to the font
Stand among the Northmen and learn what they call things
It is a feast. Sell wine
Forty pennies of linen, cut into shirts by the canons' women. The archbishop has it said from the church steps who gave it. Rollo is told too. He looks for you over the heads and nods, once.

A week on the strand among men with nothing to do but drink and wait for the rope. By the end you can ask a price, refuse one, and say what you think of a man's ship without being struck. Their children, you notice, already answer in the speech of Rouen.
You and Odilard sell from one cart, he the wine and you the carrying, to men who have never before paid for wine in this town. A hundred and fifty pennies is your part.

A bright spring day before the two joined churches of Rotomagus: an old, very big man in a long white linen garment with a small cross at his neck, an archbishop beside him; behind them a crowd of Northmen in white shirts, wet-haired; at the edge a wine cart doing good trade.
The plough left in the field

Rollo's law is short: nobody steals. He has ordered ploughs left in the furrow and gear left on the strand. He hangs the thief, and beside the thief whoever knew. This morning a bale of yours is gone from the strand.

You have heard about Longpaon? A wife there hid her own man's plough irons, to teach him to carry them home. The count paid the man five shillings for his loss, tried the whole village by hot iron, found no thief, and then asked the man whom he had told. They hanged the pair of them.
He hung gold arm rings on an oak by a pool, out in the forest. Three winters back. I rode past at Yule. They are still there, and a little green.
I know where the bale is. The net-maker's boy, two boats down. He is twelve. I saw him at first light and thought he was carrying for you. Now you know it as well, which is a pity for both of us.
If you have a thing to say, say it to me before noon. After noon it is a thing you kept.
Bring it before the count's court
Fetch the bale back yourself and say nothing
Let the bale go. Leave the rest on the strand tonight, like everybody

You say it plainly, and the mate says what he saw. The bale is found under the net-maker's floor. The judgment takes as long as a prayer: twice its worth to you, sixty pennies, out of the father's goods. The father hangs, since a boy of twelve does not hide a bale under a floor alone. The boy is given to the canons. You are thanked.

You say it badly, in the wrong order, and the net-maker says the boy carried the bale for you and you forgot. It is found; nobody hangs; you pay ten pennies for the court's morning. Ketil says you should have come before noon.

You and the mate go two boats down at dusk. The boy's mother brings the bale out before you ask, with two baskets of eels on top of it, and cannot speak. Nobody hangs. By the count's law four people on this strand now ought to.

Ketil is sitting on the bale when you get there. He has been told. He takes forty pennies from you as the price of knowing and not saying, and tells you it is the cheapest that price has ever been. The boy he sends to the canons. He does not say what is done with the father.

You know nothing, and you tell the mate he saw a boy carrying for somebody. Next morning everything of yours is where you left it, and the bale is back among it, a little damp. An old riddle about a plough is going from boat to boat along the strand; a canon writes it down for you.

Early morning on the strand at Rotomagus: bales, casks and nets lying unguarded along the whole shore; one gap in the merchant's own neat stack; the mate pointing two boats down, where a boy of twelve looks away; on the hill beyond, small, a plough standing alone in a furrow.
The archbishop's question

A crew newly come from over sea took baptism at Easter for a shirt and a length of the rope. Now there is pig's blood on the stone behind their hall, and they are selling cheap what never came off any farm. The archbishop does not know what the church does with such men. Nor does anybody.

Baptised, and some of them baptised again, and living as heathens all the while. Do I shut the door on them? Scourge them? Wait? I am writing to Hervé at Reims, who has the books and the pope's ear. Somebody must carry it up the river.
New men on his river. It is the one thing Rollo fears. If they sell plunder here, it was taken from somebody who will come looking. He would want to hear of it, and from a friend.
Wax. Good cloth. A cup or two. I do not ask where you got your boat, Frisian.
It was always going to be this. You do not wash the sea out of a man in one Easter.
Tell Ketil what the newcomers are selling
Carry the archbishop's question up the river for Reims
Buy what they sell, cheap, and ask nothing

Ketil goes up to Rollo with it. By evening the new crew's ship is hauled out and her mast unstepped: they will plough, or they will leave on foot. There are forty pennies for you, and Rollo's steward calls you by your name before other men.

You hand the letter to a clerk of Reims on the Paris strand, who has plainly been told to look for you. On the way down you spell out your own copy of the greeting by the stern lantern. The archbishop says the answer, when it comes, will be long.

Forty pennies buys two loads of wax and a bolt of altar cloth with the fringe cut off. The cloth sells the same week for a hundred and thirty; the wax is in your hold. The archbishop hears of it, as archbishops do.

Evening behind a new timber hall outside the wall: a flat stone dark with blood, a pig's head on a stake; in front, a young shipmaster with a new cross on his chest holding out a bolt of rich cloth and a cake of wax; the archbishop watching from the gate, a letter in his hand.
A length of the rope

This year the king's writing names them for the first time: the Northmen of the Seine, Rollo and his companions, to whom land was given for the keeping of the kingdom. At Rotomagus the strand below the wall is being measured out with a rope, and the wine boats lie three deep.
I speak for him. When nobody came, you came. He is measuring the strand today. He says: where does the Frisian want his rope?
Count the keels. English, Flemings, men from the Loire who a year since would have cut us down. They come because nothing is stolen here. It turns out that is all a market is.
Thorstein. I have a ship and no markets. You have markets and a boat a man could carry. Among us that is mended by joining hands.
The blades are not forgotten either. By us, kindly. By the Franks up the river, otherwise. Stay below Pîtres for a few years.
My father's forty casks a week. I passed that at Whitsun. I have stopped saying it aloud, in case God is listening.
Take a plot on the strand and a free keel
Join hands with Thorstein: his ship, your markets
Take his peace and your silver, and no land

The rope is laid from the river gate to a stake, and the stake is yours: room for a storehouse and a slip. Rollo has it said before the whole strand that your keel pays no toll at Rotomagus, in his day or his son's. Nine hundred pennies come with it: your share of the years of bread and carrying, reckoned at last.

You and Thorstein put your silver in one heap before witnesses and take it up again as one purse: fourteen hundred pennies to your side of it, the plot on the strand, the free keel, and a second ship that will sail where you send word. He cannot read a tally. He can count, and he forgets nothing.

A man with land has a lord, and you have had enough of counts. Rollo laughs, which is rare, and gives you what he gives his own shipmasters: his peace, said aloud, so that no man of his on any water lays a hand on your keel. And eleven hundred pennies.

High summer on the strand of Rotomagus, crowded with wine boats three deep: two men stretching a long rope from the river gate to a new stake; old Rollo, huge and grey, pointing with a staff; the merchant beside the stake; new timber houses rising behind the Roman wall.
The saint comes home

This year the monks of Saint Peter's came back to Rotomagus, and Saint Ouen with them, who had been carried inland out of the Northmen's way before most men now living were born. The shrine comes down the river on a barge. Your boat goes ahead of it to sound the channel.
I was a child of the cloister when the old men told us where home was. None of them lived to see it. There is no roof on the dormitory, they say. We have brought the saint and a ladder.
At Longpaon Rollo comes out on foot to meet the barge and puts his own shoulder under the shrine. So the monks say, and will go on saying.

And Reims has answered. Three and twenty chapters out of the fathers, and a letter from the pope. It comes to this: go gently. They are new. Do not break them for being what they were. I could have told myself that, but now it is written.
You carried letters when a clerk could not. The monks need a man on the strand who can sell wine and not be robbed. And I would give your house something to keep.
One letter went up to Paris, years ago, with its seal warmed. I have decided not to know about that. It will cost you a little all the same.
Keep the monks' cellar on the strand and sell their wine
Ask for a cloth that has lain on the shrine
Ask for it in writing: the archbishop's hand, the count's mark

The cellar is the old one under the south wall, dry, with a door on the strand. You hold it of Saint Peter and Saint Ouen for a tenth of what passes through, and you are the saint's man on the river: his name on your tally is worth more than a seal. Eight hundred pennies is the first year's reckoning.

The monks lay a strip of white linen on the shrine through one night's psalms and give it to you in a box of yew. It weighs nothing. Men who would not trust your oath will trust it sworn on that. Six hundred pennies besides, for the letters and the sounding.

The archbishop writes that your house served the peace of Rotomagus when it had none, and that your keel goes free at his city. Rollo, who cannot read it, has it read to him and cuts a cross under it with his own knife. With it come the cloth from the shrine and twelve hundred pennies. It is the only writing your house has that two such men agreed on.

The Seine below a wooded bend at midday: a river barge with a gabled shrine under a cloth and monks singing round it; ahead of it the merchant's small boat, a man in the bows with a sounding pole; on the bank a crowd, and one very big old man walking down to the water alone.
The river shut

The king granted nothing. The bridge at Pîtres was timbered before the frost, and at the first hard cold the Northmen's ships went down the Seine on the ebb, low in the water, and out to sea. At Parisius Count Robert's man is waiting on the strand for you.
They are gone. Some say to the Loire, some over to the English. My lord says: so long as it is somebody else's river.
Rouen? The archbishop has his city back, and his eleven canons, and grass in the market. A wall with nobody behind it. We shall put a count there when we find one who wants it.
They went with their women and burned nothing behind them. That was your asking, and my lord kept it. He says it was cheaper. From him that is thanks.
Some drowned at the bridge, trying it by night. Their friends will learn who counted the cook fires. I would keep clear of long ships for a few years.
And the matter of the iron is closed. My lord closed it himself. You will not hear of it again unless you open it.
Take the count's protection and a free keel at Paris
Ask for the river itself: the count's pilot and the marks down to the sea
Take silver and go back to the sea

Warin has it said at the count's door and written by the count's clerk: your house is under Robert's hand on the Seine and the roads beside it, and your keel pays no toll on the Paris strand. Twelve hundred pennies. The wine above the city is cheap this year, and yours to carry. There is nobody at Rouen to carry it for you.

The count's own river man takes you down from the island to the bridge and through it, and shows you every shoal and loop on the way to the tide. With that go the count's hand over your house, the free keel at Paris, and fifteen hundred pennies. No long ship has a quarrel with you. The men who left know who asked for their lives.

You ask for coin, and he is relieved: coin is easier to give than favour. Eighteen hundred pennies, and his lord's hand over your house, which costs him nothing. On the way down you pass Rotomagus without tying up. The strand is empty as far as the bend.

A cold clear winter morning on the lower Seine: a new timber bridge on old stone piers, armed men along it; beyond, far down the river, the last long ships going out small on the ebb; in front, the wall of Rotomagus with an empty strand and one small boat passing without stopping.
They say there is a market at Rouen again. The Northmen's lord there hangs thieves, takes the king's toll and no more, and the wine comes down the Seine as it did in the old days.
Saint Ouen has gone home to Rouen, on a barge, with his monks. The Northman who holds the city walked out to meet him, they say, and carried the shrine.
The Northmen have left the Seine. Count Robert barred the river at Pîtres and starved them out, and the king gave them nothing. Nobody knows which coast has them now.
